Recognize each blood cell and know its job: red cells carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets (megakaryocyte fragments) start clotting, neutrophils kill bacteria, eosinophils fight parasites and allergy, basophils hold heparin, monocytes become macrophages. Then B cells (antibodies), T cells (CD4 helpers, CD8 killers) and NK cells; the bone marrow and thymus as primary organs versus the nodes, MALT and spleen as secondary; and the layout of the thymus (cortex, medulla), lymph node (B-cell follicles, T-cell paracortex) and spleen (white pulp with its PALS of T cells around the central arteriole, red pulp). Blood holds three kinds of cells. The erythrocytes, the red blood cells, make up about 99 percent of the cells in the blood, and they carry oxygen and carbon dioxide. The platelets are fragments of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting. The rest are the white blood cells, or leukocytes: two classes, five types. 2 The white cells' jobs: the neutrophil (multi-lobed, the first line against bacteria), eosinophil (red granules, parasites and allergy), basophil (dark blue granules, heparin, asthma) and monocyte (becomes the macrophage and presents antigen on MHC II) Study guide + objectives · 8 questions in the bank Neutrophils are the main phagocyte of the blood, 50 to 70 percent of the white cells, and the body's first line of defense against bacteria. They are highly motile. They circulate in the blood for about 10 hours, then migrate into the tissues. Eosinophils and basophils both have a bilobed nucleus and IgE receptors. Tell them apart by the granules: red with eosin (the eosinophil: peroxidase and major basic protein, parasites and allergy) or dark blue to purple (the basophil: heparin and histamine, asthma). 3 B, T and NK cells: B cells (surface IgM and IgD; plasma cells make the antibodies), helper T cells (CD4, MHC II), cytotoxic T cells (CD8, perforins, allograft rejection) and NK cells (CD16 binding IgG in ADCC) Study guide + objectives · 7 questions in the bank B lymphocytes make and display membrane-bound antibodies, IgM and IgD, which act as their receptors for circulating antigens. Each mature B cell displays a single antigen-specific antibody, so it answers one antigen. A B cell can mature into a plasma cell, which makes and releases circulating antibodies. This is the humoral response. Marker CD4 CD8 Reads antigen on MHC class II MHC class I Shown it by Antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages Virus-infected and other altered cells What it does Interleukins (more CD4 cells) and lymphokines that drive B, T and NK cells; B cells need it to become plasma cells Perforins open ion channels and lyse the cell; allograft rejection and tumor immunology 4 Innate versus adaptive immunity: pre-existing barriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva, phagocytes and NK cells, versus antibodies (humoral) and T cells (cellular) Study guide + objectives · 3 questions in the bank Nonspecific, or innate, immunity is the set of pre-existing defenses against microbial invasion, in place before any contact. It has five parts: physical barriers, the skin and mucous membranes; chemical defenses, such as a low pH; secretory substances, such as lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva and interferons; phagocytic cells, the macrophages, neutrophils and monocytes; and the natural killer (NK) cells. 5 Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the bone marrow and thymus make B and T cells immunocompetent without antigen (B and NK cells mature in the marrow, T cells in the thymus); lymph nodes, MALT and the spleen activate them Study guide + objectives · 4 questions in the bank The primary lymphoid organs, the bone marrow and the thymus, develop immunocompetent B and T cells in the absence of antigen. The blood and lymph carry those cells to the secondary lymphoid organs, and B and T cells are activated by antigen in the secondary, or peripheral, organs. 6 The spleen's white and red pulp: T cells in the PALS around the central arteriole, the marginal zone of macrophages and some B cells, red pulp of splenic cords and sinusoids, no cortex or medulla, no afferent lymphatics, and what the spleen does Study guide + objectives · 7 questions in the bank The spleen filters blood and responds to systemic, blood-borne infections. It lies in the upper left quadrant of the abdomen, behind the stomach and just below the diaphragm. In adults it is the largest lymphoid organ, about the size of a clenched fist. At its hilum, the splenic artery, which carries in the blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes, enters with the nerves, and the splenic vein and lymphatics leave. It has no afferent lymphatics; its efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum. The white pulp is islands of lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole, which comes from the splenic artery after many treelike branchings. The lymphocytes wrapped around the arteriole form the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath, the PALS, and they are mainly T cells. Lymphoid nodules lie farther out in the white pulp, and they are the B cells: primary nodules, or secondary ones with germinal centers, as in the lymph nodes. A nodule pushes the arteriole off to one side. Around the white pulp is a shell of sparsely cellular lymphoid tissue, the marginal zone, with macrophages and some B cells. 7 The thymus: the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla with Hassall's corpuscles, its epithelioreticular stroma, the three layers of the blood-thymus barrier, no afferent lymphatics, and involution to fat from the early teens Study guide + objectives · 5 questions in the bank It is largest and most active in the newborn and before adolescence: about 12 to 15 grams at birth and 30 to 40 grams by puberty. By the early teens it starts to shrink, which is thymic involution, and adipose (fat) tissue replaces it. The medulla is the inner part of the lobule. It has more epithelioreticular cells, with pale nuclei, and loosely packed T cells, and it stains lighter because its T cells are bigger and less crowded. Its distinguishing feature is the Hassall's corpuscles: concentric layers of flattened epithelial cells that stain acidophilic (pink). Macrophages and dendritic cells are found in both regions. 8 The lymph node: afferent and efferent lymphatics, B cells in the cortex follicles and germinal centers, T cells in the paracortex, blood lymphocytes entering through high endothelial venules, and what a node does Study guide + objectives · 6 questions in the bank Reticular cells make and secrete the type III collagen and the matrix that form the stroma. Lymphocytes also arrive from the blood. Blood comes in through an artery at the hilum, and its lymphocytes cross into the deep cortex through the high endothelial venules, HEVs. T cells and dendritic cells are directed to the paracortex, and B cells to the cortex. Both leave the node through the efferent lymphatic vessel. The lymph node is the only lymphoid structure with both afferent and efferent lymphatics. 9 T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, positive selection in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla, single CD4 or CD8 cells out, and 95 to 99 percent dying by apoptosis Study guide + objectives · 2 questions in the bank Then come two tests. In the cortex, the epithelioreticular cells present antigen on MHC molecules: a thymocyte whose receptor recognizes them survives, and one that doesn't dies. This is positive selection. The survivors move into the medulla for negative selection, which eliminates the cells aimed at self antigen displayed on self MHC. The cells that pass both become CD8-positive cytotoxic or CD4-positive helper T cells, ready for an immune response, and they leave through postcapillary venules into the circulation. 10 Blood through the spleen: sheathed capillaries emptying into the splenic cords (the open circulation), and the slit-walled sinuses the cells squeeze back into Study guide + objectives · 2 questions in the bank In the open circulation, the sheathed capillaries empty directly into the reticular meshwork of the splenic cords rather than connecting to the endothelium-lined sinuses. The blood seeps slowly between the cords, where macrophages sample it, then reenters the circulation through the splenic sinuses. In the closed route, capillaries drain straight into the sinuses. The splenic sinuses are special sinusoidal vessels. They are lined by rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells that run lengthwise, with slit-like spaces between them, and macrophage processes reach between the cells to monitor the passing blood for foreign antigens. They have only strands of basal lamina, which loop around the endothelial cells at right angles, like the hoops around the staves of a leaky barrel. They have no smooth muscle and no pericytes. Blood cells move across the wall by squeezing through the slits. 11 MALT and the tonsils: M cells carrying antigen into the Peyer's patches, IgA into the lumen, and adenoiditis of the pharyngeal tonsil Core of the slides · 3 questions in the bank M cells are the epithelial cells that cover the Peyer's patches, and they are antigen-transporting cells. They take up microorganisms and macromolecules from the lumen in endocytic vesicles, carry them to their basolateral membrane, and release them near the B cells and CD4-positive T cells. Macrophages under the epithelium then process the material and present it.
